input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was investigated by means of batch tests carried out at 298 K. In a batch test of this kind, a fixed volume of the dye solution is brought into contact with a known mass of the adsorbent and the concentration remaining in the solution is followed over time. The capacity of the carbon was characterised by fitting the Langmuir relation to the measured data, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was found to be 123 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5, this parameter representing the saturation capacity of the adsorbent under the conditions of the fit. In a further test, an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1 was employed, and it was found that the removal achieved after 120 min amounted to 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, which means that the concentration remaining in solution at that point was 6.5 mg L-1. The capacity and the removal describe different aspects of the performance of the carbon: the capacity is a property of the adsorbent as characterised by the fit, expressed per gram of the material, whereas the removal is the outcome obtained in a particular test at a particular dose and contact time. It should be noted that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only, and that the capacity at other pH values was not measured, so that the capacity figure quoted here cannot be assumed to apply at other values of pH.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. In a batch test a fixed volume of dye solution is contacted with a known mass of adsorbent and the concentration left in solution is followed over time. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 123 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. The Langmuir capacity is the saturation capacity parameter of the fitted relation, and the value belongs to the fit at the stated pH. At an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, and the concentration left in solution was 6.5 mg L-1. The dose states the mass of adsorbent per unit volume of solution treated, and the removal is stated against the initial concentration as its denominator, at the stated contact time. The removal belongs to the stated dose and the stated contact time jointly: it is the outcome of the test as run, not a property of the carbon alone. The capacity, by contrast, is a property of the adsorbent as the fit characterises it, stated per gram of adsorbent, and the two figures answer different questions about the same material. One gives the uptake the fitted relation assigns to the carbon at saturation; the other gives the share of the dye that a stated dose removed from a stated solution in a stated time. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the capacity figure is limited to the pH at which the fit was made.
